text.name: Minimum password length
text.titlePass: Passwords must be at least 14 characters
text.why: Short passwords are guessed quickly once an attacker has the password file. This applies to accounts kept on this PC.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
On a single PC, open secpol.msc > Account Policies > Password Policy and set Minimum password length to 14.

text.name: Password history
text.why: Without a password history, a changed password can be switched straight back to the old, possibly leaked, one.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
On a single PC, open secpol.msc > Account Policies > Password Policy and set Enforce password history to 24.

text.name: Account lockout
text.titlePass: Accounts lock after repeated wrong passwords
text.titleFail: Accounts do not lock after wrong passwords
text.why: Without lockout, a program can try passwords against this PC without end until one works.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
On a single PC, open secpol.msc > Account Policies > Account Lockout Policy and set the threshold to 10.

text.name: Lockout time
text.titlePass: Locked accounts stay locked long enough
text.why: A lockout that ends after a moment barely slows down password guessing.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
On a single PC, open secpol.msc > Account Policies > Account Lockout Policy and set the duration to 10 minutes or more.

text.name: Accounts without a password
text.titlePass: Accounts without a password cannot sign in over the network
text.titleFail: Accounts without a password can sign in over the network
text.why: An account with no password is harmless only as long as it can be used at the keyboard alone.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
On a single PC, open secpol.msc > Local Policies > Security Options and enable the blank passwords setting under Accounts.

registry.item: Blank passwords limited to the keyboard

text.name: Administrator prompt
text.titlePass: Windows asks before giving administrator rights
text.titleFail: Administrator rights are given without asking
text.why: When Windows elevates without a prompt, any program run by an administrator silently gets full control of the PC.
fix: Open Start, type UAC and open Change User Account Control settings.
Move the slider up from the bottom position and select OK.
If the slider is locked, the setting comes from your organisation: tell IT.

onlyWhen.otherwise: User Account Control is off, so no prompt is shown at all; see the User Account Control check.

registry.expected: Asks for consent or a password

labels.1: Asks for a password on the secure desktop
labels.2: Asks for consent on the secure desktop
labels.5: Asks for consent for programs that are not part of Windows

absent.found: Not configured (Windows default: asks for consent)

text.name: Secure desktop for prompts
text.titlePass: Administrator prompts appear on the secure desktop
text.titleFail: Administrator prompts appear on the normal desktop
text.why: On the normal desktop, another program can click or imitate the administrator prompt. The secure desktop shuts every other program out.
fix: Open Start, type UAC and open Change User Account Control settings.
Choose one of the two upper positions, which dim the desktop, and select OK.

onlyWhen.otherwise: User Account Control is off, so no prompt is shown at all; see the User Account Control check.

text.name: Built-in Administrator and prompts
text.titlePass: The built-in Administrator is asked before elevation too
text.titleFail: The built-in Administrator is never asked before elevation
text.why: If the built-in Administrator account is ever enabled, everything it runs has full control at once. It matters little while that account is off.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
On a single PC, open secpol.msc > Local Policies > Security Options and enable Admin Approval Mode for the Built-in Administrator account.
